culturalStory.heading: About the Raven
body: The raven (kahkakiw) holds significant cultural importance in many Indigenous traditions, including Plains Cree (nēhiyawēwin). Known for its intelligence, adaptability, problem-solving ability, and distinctive black plumage and rasping call, the raven appears in numerous oral stories and teachings.

In Cree storytelling the raven is often a trickster and messenger figure — a bird that watches, remembers, and carries news between worlds. This trail sign honours that presence with a stylized black raven silhouette and the syllabics ᑲᐦᑲᑭᐤ set across its body in red, so that the Cree name is literally carried on the raven itself.

notes: Sign text verified visually from docs/assets/kahkakiw/raven_wild.png: SRO 'kahkakiw' (black, top), syllabics 'ᑲᐦᑲᑭᐤ' (red, on raven body), 'RAVEN' (black, bottom). Sign primary colours are white plaque, black silhouette+lettering, red syllabics.

culturalStory.heading: Spine of the Trail
body: In mountain-bike vernacular, a trail earns the name Back Breaker by feel — by the rooty, rattling sections that hammer your spine through the bars, by the line that punishes a lazy posture and rewards a loose grip. The trail of that name drops through MacKinnon Ravine on Edmonton's west side as the rooty companion to Root Canal: short, sharp, and unforgiving enough that the name has stuck for years among the local riders who built and maintain it.

The plaque leans into the joke literally. A single white vertebra dangles like a charm against the black field, ringed with red the way a sore spine glows after a hard run. The accompanying parts in this sign's set — a five-vertebra column and a length of chain — push the pun further: a backbone built like a bike chain, each link a vertebra, the rider's spine and the bike's drivetrain merged into one rattling assembly. Red on black is the working-shop palette of grease, rust, and warning tape; the white SRO and English text keep the language clearly legible against it.

The Cree reading kaskâwikanênêw carries that same idea in its own register — a verb built from kaskâ‑ ‘to snap, break across’ and the body-part medial ‑wikan‑ ‘back, spine’: literally, ‘s/he breaks his/her back (by hand).’ The syllabics above the SRO are picked out in the same red as the vertebra's accents, so the language and the image read as a single gesture. The sign sits on ᓀᐦᐃᔭᐤ ᐊᐢᑭᕀ Nêhiyaw‑Askiy (Plains Cree territory), and is part of an Edmonton-area effort to put Plains Cree names back on the everyday landscape of trails that riders here have known by their English nicknames for a long time.

notes: PHYSICAL SIGN OVERRIDES CATALOGUE: The plaque is carved with SRO 'kaskâwikanênêw' (circumflex on the third 'a') and syllabics 'ᑲᐢᑳᐏᑲᓀᓀᐤ' (long-â dot on the third glyph ᑳ). The current catalogue.json has 'kaskawikanênêw' / 'ᑲᐢᑲᐏᑲᓀᓀᐤ' — both missing the long-â diacritic in matched positions. The plaque is internally consistent and matches the itwêwina (Wolvengrey/CW) headword 'kaskâwikanênêw' = 's/he breaks s.o.’s back by hand'. Coordinator should update catalogue.json creeName + creeSyllabics to match the plaque when merging.

Photo placeholder pending — user to provide a dedicated 'docs/assets/backbreaker/' image, or crop the plaque from allSigns.jpg. The 'photo' field is intentionally left as {} so the renderer falls back to the three.js STL embed.

Morpheme bracketing of the verb tail '-n-êw' is one of two defensible analyses; an alternative is to collapse '-ê-n-êw' into a single VTA 3→3′ ‘by hand’ suffix. Either reading is linguistically valid; the 5-morpheme split is used here for teaching clarity.
The medial '-wikan-' is the body-part-incorporated form of the free noun 'wîkan' (long î). The shortening to short i in medial position is standard Plains Cree behavior.

relatedForms[2] (kaskâwikanisin, ‘s/he has a broken back from falling’) is reconstructed from the kaskâ- result list rather than confirmed by a single-word lookup; spelling carries roughly 80% confidence. May be replaced or dropped on user review.
mispiskwan syllabics use the decomposed form 'ᒥᐢᐱᐢᑲᐧᐣ'; the unified-syllabics combining form 'ᒁ' for 'kwa' is also valid. Pick whichever matches the rest of the site's convention.

The visible plaque on the wall shows only the dangling vertebra; the project STL set includes a 5-vertebra column and a chain motif which may belong to a larger composite design or a future installation.

Trailforks pick: 'Back Breaker' (trailId 10634), Hawrelak / MacKinnon Ravine, Northwest Edmonton — companion to Root Canal. A 'Lower Back Breaker' sibling trail also exists in the same network but is almost certainly not what the plaque commemorates.

culturalStory.heading: About kâkwa — the Porcupine
body: kâkwa (ᑳᑿ) is the Cree word for porcupine — a slow-moving, deeply self-possessed forest dweller of the boreal woods that stretch across nêhiyaw (Cree) territory. Unhurried and largely solitary, the porcupine is famously well-defended: rather than fight or flee, it lowers its head, raises its quills, and lets any aggressor make the mistake of pressing in. Cree teachings often hold up kâkwa as a quiet model of patience and gentle strength — protection through stillness rather than aggression, and the wisdom of knowing when not to move.

Long before glass beads arrived through the fur trade, porcupine quillwork was one of the most refined craft traditions of the Plains and Woodlands peoples, including the Cree. Quills were plucked, soaked, dyed with pigments drawn from roots, berries, lichens and ochres, then softened in the mouth, flattened with the teeth, and woven, wrapped, or sewn onto tanned hide, birchbark, moccasins, pipe stems, and lidded boxes. The geometric and floral patterns that later flourished in beadwork were first carried by quills — making kâkwa not only a forest neighbour but a literal source of artistic material, generously offered by an animal that asked only to be approached with care.

The red, black, and white of this trail sign carry an echo of those older quill-dye palettes — earth reds, charcoal blacks, and undyed natural whites that recur across many Indigenous quillwork traditions. (We note this resonance gently, as a visual rhyme rather than a claim about any specific tribal recipe.) Riding past kâkwa here in the river valley, it is worth pausing to remember an animal that taught generations of artists how to make beauty out of patience, and how to defend a small life with quiet, deliberate care.

notes: Spelling discrepancy: catalogue currently records creeName "kakwa" and creeSyllabics "ᑲᑲᐧ", but the carved sign reads SRO "kâkwa" (circumflex on first a, high confidence) and syllabics best-read as "ᑳᑿ" (left glyph ᑳ confirmed by long-vowel dot; right glyph ᑿ chosen to match carved Roman "kwa", with bare ᑲ as secondary possibility at the photo resolution available). pageContent uses the carved form per the manager brief (trust the sign first).

Recommend the coordinator update catalogue.json creeName → "kâkwa" and creeSyllabics → "ᑳᑿ" when merging, so the catalogue summary matches the carved plaque. Flagging for curator review rather than editing catalogue here.

Second syllabic glyph (ka vs kwa) could not be resolved to certainty from the composite allSigns.jpg crop. A high-resolution single-panel photo would confirm whether the carved form is ᑳᑿ (kâ-kwa) or ᑳᑲ (kâ-ka). Best read used here: ᑳᑿ.

Trailforks: no Edmonton-area MTB trail named Kakwa, Kâkwa, or Porcupine was found across six search queries and direct grepping of trailforks.com Edmonton region pages on 2026-05-14. Only namesake is Kakwa Wildland Provincial Park near Grande Prairie (~160 km SW), an OHV/hike area geographically unrelated to Edmonton. trailforks left as {}; the sign likely commemorates the Cree word as cultural/linguistic content rather than naming an existing trail segment. Search was web-based, not Trailforks API-direct, so confidence is ~90% not 100%.
